A.explanation: Since $1 \text{V} = 1 \text{J C}^{-1}$, $2 \text{ } \mu\text{J C}^{-1} = 2 \text{ } \mu\text{V}$, which is 1000 times smaller than $2000 \text{ } \mu\text{V}$.

C.explanation: $2 \text{ pV} = 2 \times 10^{-12} \text{ V}$, which is much smaller than $2000 \times 10^{-6} \text{ V}$.

D.explanation: $2000 \text{ mV} = 2 \text{ V}$, which is 1000 times larger than $2000 \text{ } \mu\text{V}$.

hints: Notice the starting value is $2000$ microvolts, where micro means $10^{-6}$, so write it as $2000 \times 10^{-6} \text{ V}$.
Recall that milli means $10^{-3}$, so ask how many $10^{-3} \text{ V}$ fit into $2000 \times 10^{-6} \text{ V}$.
Check option A by using $1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J C}^{-1}$, so $\mu\text{J C}^{-1}$ is the same size as $\mu\text{V}$.
walkthrough: Start with the given quantity: $2000$ microvolts $= 2000 \text{ } \mu\text{V}$.
Use SI prefixes: $1 \text{ } \mu\text{V} = 10^{-6} \text{ V}$ and $1 \text{ mV} = 10^{-3} \text{ V}$.
Recognise $2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ V}$ as $2 \text{ mV}$ because $10^{-3}$ corresponds to milli.
